extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy; legislators and political theorists
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of Aristotle's Politics (books on citizenship and constitutions) concerning the nature of the city, citizenship, virtues, and the correct loci and forms of government. Focuses on normative criteria for what makes a city, who are citizens, and what government is just.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a citizen
rubrics_metrics.description: A citizen is one who exercises certain offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats citizenship in terms of participation in public offices; even an illegally created person who performs the offices continues to be a citizen (though whether justly or unjustly is another question).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts of the city are acts of those managing public affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: When anything is done by those who have the management of public affairs where a democracy (or other constitution) is established, their actions are to be considered as the actions of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies across regimes (democracy, oligarchy, tyranny); disputes (e.g., refusal to fulfil contracts after a regime change) should be treated as public/state acts when performed by public managers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sameness of a city depends on its constitution/government
rubrics_metrics.description: When we speak of a city as being the same we refer to the government there established, not merely the place, walls, or even the same inhabitants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: a chorus with same performers can be a different species (tragic vs comic); likewise the species of constitution determines identity. Whether to dissolve the community when the constitution is altered is a separate question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of political inquiry includes extent and composition of a city
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining how large a city should be and whether it may consist of more than one people are particulars the politician should not be unacquainted with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical matters (place, inhabitants) are solvable in many ways; the political theorist must be aware of these particulars when defining cities and constitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue of a citizen is referred to the state and differs by constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The virtue of a citizen has necessarily a reference to the state; actions constituting an excellent citizen in one community will not constitute it in another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because cities require different roles (like sailors with different appointments), citizen-virtue is role-relative. Therefore the virtues that make a 'good man' are not identical with those that make an 'excellent citizen' across all states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impossibility of a city of uniformly excellent citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible that a city should consist entirely of excellent citizens because citizens have different callings and qualifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A city is composed of dissimilar parts (analogy to animal/household), so the virtues of citizens must vary; perfection of the city arises from the proper exercise of varied excellences, not uniform human excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulers may need specialized education
rubrics_metrics.description: Those intended to command should have an education different from other citizens (e.g., children of kings taught riding and warlike exercises).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some legislators argue for a distinctive upbringing for rulers; reference to Euripides: 'teach me what the state requires.' This supports differentiated civic education where necessary for effective rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good citizen should know how to command and obey
rubrics_metrics.description: A commendable citizen knows both how to command and how to obey; being able to do both well is the virtue of an accomplished citizen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: generals must have served under command; the governed should know how freemen ought to govern as well as be governed. This dual capacity distinguishes accomplished citizens from those only fitted for one role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion/ Inclusion of mechanics as citizens depends on state type
rubrics_metrics.description: There is doubt whether mechanics (handicraftsmen, hired servants) are to be considered citizens; best-regulated states often exclude mechanics from citizenship, though democracies may admit them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanics who labour for hire or live servile lives are often considered unfit for public office; some states require a waiting period (e.g., Thebes: ten years out of trade) before sharing government. Inclusion often responds to population scarcity or differing conceptions of civic virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: A city is a community for living well (happiness), not merely for safety or commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: A city is a society of people joining together with families and children to live agreeably for the sake of a perfect independent life — to live well and happily, not merely to preserve life or trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences of this definition: law aims at citizens' virtues; mere alliances for defence or commercial treaties do not make a city. Social institutions (marriage, clubs, sacrifices) foster the friendship/sociability required for living well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governments aimed at common good are just; those aimed at rulers' good are unjust
rubrics_metrics.description: All those governments which have a common good in view are rightly established and strictly just; those which aim only at the good of the rulers are founded on wrong principles (tyranny over freemen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes legitimate government (serving the common good) from forms that are corrupt or unjust because they serve particular interests of rulers or classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of basic regimes by who holds supreme power for the common good
rubrics_metrics.description: When supreme power is in one for the common good it is a kingdom; when in a few it is an aristocracy (governed by the most worthy); when in the whole people for the common good it is a state (polity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each of these proper forms can degenerate into corrupt forms: kingdom→tyranny, aristocracy→oligarchy, state→democracy (as corruption). The definition is tied to whether rulers consult the common good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of corrupt regimes by whose good they consult
rubrics_metrics.description: A tyranny is a monarchy where the good of one man only is the object of government; an oligarchy considers only the rich; a democracy considers only the poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corruption is judged by whether government serves private interest rather than the common good. The label (tyrant/oligarch/democrat) hinges on whose benefit is privileged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchy vs democracy depends on wealth of those governing, not mere numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference between oligarchy and democracy is not simply the number (few or many) but whether the rulers are the rich or the poor: government in hands of the rich (few or many) is oligarchy; in hands of the poor is democracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because rich are normally few and poor many, number and wealth correlate, but the defining feature is the economic status of rulers rather than numerical majority alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice is relative to the persons judged (equality varies by who is equal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice has reference to persons: what is equal appears just among equals; what is unequal appears just among unequals; disputes often arise from neglecting this relational character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political debates about distribution (e.g., shares of power relative to fortune) reflect differing views about whether the city was founded to preserve property vs to enable living well; each side asserts a partial justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power should be shared with the many to some degree
rubrics_metrics.description: The supreme power ought to be lodged with the many rather than with the few; although not every individual of the many may be fit, collectively they may be better qualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments: the many bring diverse virtues and wisdom; the crowd can judge collectively (e.g., public tastes); practical compromise: let the many vote in assemblies, determine causes, elect officers and inquire into conduct, but prevent them from holding certain magistracies directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of excluding the many (necessity of some share of power)
rubrics_metrics.description: If many poor people are incapable of acquiring honours and are given no share in government, the state will necessarily have many enemies within it; some participation is therefore necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended measures: permit voting, deliberation, election power, and scrutiny of officers' conduct to integrate the many while reserving high offices to those of fortune and worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert selection principle vs collective judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: One principle: those skilled in an art should select practitioners (e.g., physicians judged by physicians); counterprinciple: collective bodies of non-experts can collectively judge better in many cases (householder better judge of his house than builder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to elections and judgments: there is a tension between entrusting elections/censure to specialists versus to the people. Aristotle weighs both: specialists have technical knowledge, while the mixed capacities of the many can yield better collective judgments in some domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law should govern, not arbitrary man
rubrics_metrics.description: It is wrong to let a man have the supreme power and not the law, because man is subject to passions; law restrains personal caprice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if law establishes an aristocracy or democracy, law's authority is preferable to arbitrary personal rule. This supports constitutional constraints over rule by persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic offices are honours and must be distributed to preserve public esteem
rubrics_metrics.description: The offices of a city are its honours; if one set of men are always in power, the rest will be unhonoured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a political-psychological consideration motivating some share of offices for different classes to maintain civic cohesion and esteem.
